course: Petrol and Diesel Engine Fundamentals: 0 to 12 Litres

lessons.title: Thermodynamics of Combustion
lessons.body: When you burn petrol or diesel in an engine, you are turning chemical energy into heat, and then heat into motion. This is thermodynamics. In a petrol engine, the spark plug ignites a mixture of air and fuel. The burning gas expands rapidly, pushing the piston down. That push is what turns the crankshaft. In a diesel engine, the air is squeezed so hard it becomes hot enough to ignite the diesel when it is injected. No spark plug needed. The key numbers: petrol has a stoichiometric ratio of about 14.7 parts air to 1 part fuel by weight. Diesel is about 14.5:1. But diesel engines run leanâoften 18:1 to 70:1âbecause they control power by how much fuel is injected, not by throttling air. Petrol engines need a throttle to control air, so they always try to stay near 14.7:1 for clean burning. In Africa, where fuel quality varies, running slightly rich (12.5:1 to 13:1) can help cool the engine and prevent knock, but it wastes fuel and fouls plugs. The three laws of thermodynamics matter: energy cannot be created or destroyed; heat always flows from hot to cold; and you can never get 100% efficiency. A typical petrol engine is about 25-30% efficient. Diesel is 30-40%. The rest is lost as heat out the exhaust and radiator. To feel this, touch the exhaust manifold after a short runâit will be hundreds of degrees. That heat came from your fuel. Mechanics in Nairobi or Lagos often see engines overheating because the cooling system cannot remove that heat fast enough. Understanding this helps you diagnose: if an engine runs hot, check ignition timing, fuel mixture, and coolant flow. If it runs cold, check the thermostat. Combustion is not magicâit is controlled burning that you can measure with a timing light, a compression gauge, and a exhaust gas analyser.

lessons.title: Air-Fuel Mixtures and Stoichiometry
lessons.body: Stoichiometry is the exact ratio of air to fuel that burns completely with nothing left over. For petrol, that is 14.7 kilograms of air to 1 kilogram of fuel. For diesel, it is about 14.5:1. But engines rarely run at exactly that ratio all the time. Petrol engines use a throttle plate to control how much air enters. The engine control unit (ECU) then adds fuel to match. At idle, you might have 14.7:1. At full throttle, you might go rich to 12.5:1 for more power. At cruise, you might go lean to 15.5:1 for economy. In Africa, where many vehicles are older and have carburettors, you adjust the mixture screw by hand. A good starting point is to turn the screw in until the engine stumbles, then out one and a half turns. Use a vacuum gauge: highest vacuum at idle means best mixture. For diesel, there is no throttle. Air is always unrestricted. You control power by how much fuel the injection pump delivers. So a diesel can run very leanâ30:1 or more at idle. That is why diesels are more efficient. But too lean at high load can melt pistons. Too rich wastes fuel and makes black smoke. To check mixture on a petrol engine, use a colour tune or an exhaust gas analyser. On a diesel, look at the exhaust: black smoke means too much fuel, white smoke means unburnt fuel or water, blue smoke means oil burning. In many African workshops, you can use a simple Gunson Gastester or even a narrowband oxygen sensor with a multimeter. The goal is to keep the mixture in a range that gives good power, acceptable economy, and does not damage the engine. Remember: air is free, fuel costs money. Running slightly lean saves fuel but can raise exhaust gas temperatures. Running rich wastes fuel but cools the engine. Find the balance for your conditionsâdusty roads, high altitude, or poor fuel quality.

lessons.title: Compression Ratios and Their Effects
lessons.body: Compression ratio is the volume of the cylinder when the piston is at the bottom divided by the volume when it is at the top. A petrol engine typically has a compression ratio of 8:1 to 12:1. A diesel engine has 14:1 to 23:1. Higher compression means more power and better efficiency because the air-fuel mixture is squeezed into a smaller space, so the burn is faster and more complete. But higher compression also means more heat and more risk of knock in petrol engines. In Africa, many older petrol engines run 8.5:1 to 9.5:1 because fuel octane is often low (91 or 93 RON). If you increase compression without increasing octane, you get knockâa pinging sound that can destroy pistons. Diesel engines use high compression to ignite the fuel. The air is compressed so much it reaches 700-900Â°C. That is why diesel engines are heavier and noisier. To measure compression, you need a compression gauge. Remove all spark plugs or injectors, screw the gauge into one cylinder, hold the throttle wide open, and crank the engine 4-6 times. A healthy petrol engine should read 10-14 bar (150-200 psi). A diesel should read 20-30 bar (300-450 psi). Low compression means worn rings, valves, or head gasket. In many African workshops, you can borrow a compression gauge from a tool library or buy a basic one for $20. If one cylinder is low, pour a teaspoon of oil into it and retest. If compression rises, the rings are worn. If it stays low, the valves are leaking. Compression ratio also affects fuel choice. High compression engines need high-octane fuel. In countries where only low-octane fuel is available, you must retard ignition timing to prevent knock. That is why some cars have a switch for 'regular' or 'premium' fuel. Understanding compression helps you diagnose power loss, rough idle, and overheating. It is the heart of engine health.

lessons.title: Ignition Timing and Combustion Phasing
lessons.body: Ignition timing is when the spark plug fires in a petrol engine. It is measured in degrees before top dead centre (BTDC). If the spark fires too early, the burning mixture pushes against the rising piston, causing knock and power loss. If it fires too late, the burn finishes after the piston is already going down, so you lose power and overheat the exhaust. A typical petrol engine idles at 8-12Â° BTDC and advances to 30-40Â° BTDC at high rpm. The engine control unit (ECU) adjusts timing based on engine speed, load, and knock sensor signals. On older engines with a distributor, you set base timing with a timing light. Connect the light to cylinder 1 spark plug wire, point it at the crankshaft pulley, and turn the distributor until the mark lines up with the specified degreesâoften 10Â° BTDC with the vacuum advance disconnected. In Africa, many mechanics use a simple inductive timing light that costs $30. If you do not have one, you can set timing by ear: advance until the engine starts to knock, then back off slightly. But that is risky. Better to use a light. For diesel engines, there is no spark. Ignition happens when fuel is injected into hot compressed air. The timing is controlled by the injection pump. You adjust it by rotating the pump slightly. Too advanced and you get diesel knock (harsh noise). Too retarded and you get white smoke and poor power. In modern common-rail diesels, the ECU controls injection timing precisely. Combustion phasing is about when the peak pressure occurs. Ideally, it should be about 10-15Â° after top dead centre. That gives maximum push on the piston. If peak pressure is too early, you waste energy fighting the piston. If too late, you lose heat to the exhaust. You can check phasing with a pressure transducer, but that is expensive. Instead, listen to the engine: smooth and quiet means good phasing. Rough and noisy means timing is off. Always check timing after replacing a timing belt or distributor.

lessons.title: Knock and Pre-Ignition in Petrol Engines
lessons.body: Knock and pre-ignition are two different problems that sound similar but have different causes. Knock happens after the spark plug fires. The flame front moves across the cylinder, but the unburned mixture ahead of it gets so hot and compressed that it explodes spontaneously. That creates a sharp pressure spike that hits the piston like a hammer. You hear a pinging or rattling sound. Pre-ignition happens before the spark. Something hot in the cylinderâlike a glowing spark plug tip, a carbon deposit, or an overheated valveâignites the mixture early. That tries to push the piston down while it is still coming up. The engine loses power and can be destroyed quickly. Knock is usually caused by low-octane fuel, too much ignition advance, high compression, or a lean mixture. Pre-ignition is caused by hot spots, wrong spark plugs, or overheating. In Africa, knock is common because fuel octane can be as low as 91 RON. If your car needs 95 RON and you use 91, you must retard timing by 2-4 degrees. You can also use a fuel additive, but that is expensive. Better to set timing correctly. To diagnose knock, use a knock sensor or a stethoscope. A simple trick: accelerate hard in third gear from low rpm. If you hear pinging, you have knock. Pre-ignition is harder to hear because it happens at high rpm. It often sounds like a distant metallic rattle. If you suspect pre-ignition, check spark plug heat range. A hotter plug can cause pre-ignition. Use a colder plug if you drive hard. Also check for carbon buildup. In many African cities, fuel quality is inconsistent, so carbon builds up fast. You can clean it with a fuel system cleaner or by removing the head and scraping. Never ignore knock or pre-ignition. They can hole a piston in minutes. If you hear either, back off the throttle, check timing, and use the correct octane fuel. If you cannot get high-octane fuel, retard timing and keep rpm moderate.

lessons.title: Diesel Combustion and Ignition Delay
lessons.body: Diesel combustion works differently from petrol. There is no spark plug. Air is drawn into the cylinder and compressed to a ratio of 14:1 to 23:1. That compression heats the air to 700-900Â°C. At the end of compression, the injector sprays diesel fuel directly into the hot air. The fuel does not burn immediately. There is a short delayâcalled ignition delayâwhile the fuel vaporises and mixes with air. That delay is typically 1-2 milliseconds. During that time, the fuel sprays into the cylinder and mixes. Then, when the mixture reaches its autoignition temperature, it ignites all at once. That causes a rapid pressure rise and the characteristic diesel clatter. If ignition delay is too long, too much fuel has mixed, and the sudden burn is violentâthat is diesel knock. If delay is too short, the fuel may not mix well, causing incomplete combustion and black smoke. To control ignition delay, you need good injectors, correct injection timing, and the right cetane number fuel. Cetane is the diesel equivalent of octane. Higher cetane means shorter delay. In Africa, diesel cetane can be 45-50. That is acceptable. But if you get poor fuel, delay increases and the engine knocks. You can adjust injection timing to compensate. On a mechanical injection pump, rotate the pump slightly toward the engine to advance timing (shorter delay) or away to retard. On common-rail, the ECU does it. To diagnose diesel combustion problems, look at the exhaust. White smoke means unburnt fuelâoften from retarded timing or bad injectors. Black smoke means too much fuel or not enough airâcheck the air filter and turbo. Blue smoke means oil burning. A simple test for injectors is a pop tester. You can also use a diesel compression gauge. In many African workshops, you can test injectors by cracking the injector line one at a time while the engine runs. If the engine note does not change, that cylinder is weak. Ignition delay is also affected by engine temperature. Cold engines have longer delay, which is why they clatter more and need glow plugs. Once warm, delay shortens and the engine runs smoother. Always use the correct grade of diesel and change fuel filters regularly.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Engine Operating Principles for African Agribusiness & Transport Fleets

This practical reference distils the six theory lessons of Engine Operating Principles into field-usable guidance for African operators running 0â12 litre petrol and diesel engines. Whether you manage a maize milling line in Nakuru, a fleet of 3-tonne Isuzu NKR delivery trucks in Kumasi, a borehole irrigation pump in the Zambezi valley, or a 12-litre Scania hauling copper out of the Copperbelt, the same physical laws govern your fuel bill, your maintenance interval, and your uptime. This module is written business-first: every principle is tied to cost, reliability, or revenue.

Why Operating Principles Are a Profit Centre, Not a Theory Lesson

In most African agribusiness operations, fuel and lubricants consume 35â60% of total operating cost for engine-driven assets. A single mis-timed injection pump or a leaking intercooler can raise specific fuel consumption by 8â15%, which on a 500-litre-per-day operation is the difference between profit and loss. Understanding combustion thermodynamics, air-fuel ratios, compression, ignition timing, and knock lets a workshop foreman diagnose by symptom rather than by parts-swapping â the single biggest hidden cost in African workshops where genuine spares are expensive and lead times are long.

The six lessons map directly onto six field decisions:

  • Thermodynamics of Combustion â why exhaust gas temperature (EGT) is your cheapest engine health sensor.
  • Air-Fuel Mixtures & Stoichiometry â why dust-clogged filters silently destroy fuel economy.
  • Compression Ratios â why a worn engine is hard to start cold and smoky when hot.
  • Ignition Timing & Combustion Phasing â why petrol engines ping on low-octane fuel.
  • Knock & Pre-Ignition â why "engine knock" is a money leak, not a noise nuisance.
  • Diesel Combustion & Ignition Delay â why diesel clatter changes when fuel quality drops.

Data Table 1: Typical Operating Parameters â Petrol vs Diesel (0â12 L Class)

Parameter Petrol (SI) engine Diesel (CI) engine Field implication (Africa)

Stoichiometric AFR (mass)â 14.7:1â 14.5:1Air filter restriction hits both, but diesel smokes first
Ignition triggerSpark plug (timed)Injection (compression heat)Petrol timing is adjustable; diesel timing is pump/injector-set
Peak cylinder pressure40 â 60 bar60 â 90 bar (naturally aspirated)Higher diesel pressure demands better fuel quality
Typical thermal efficiency25 â 32%35 â 45%Diesel wins on fuel cost per tonne-km
EGT at full load700 â 900 Â°C500 â 700 Â°C (pre-turbo)EGT gauge is the cheapest early-warning device
Knock sensitivityHigh (octane-dependent)Low (cetane-dependent)Fuel quality variance across African supply chains matters

Source: Compiled from Heywood (1988), Internal Combustion Engine Fundamentals, McGraw-Hill, Ch. 1 & 2; and Bosch (2018), Automotive Handbook, 10th ed., Robert Bosch GmbH.

Data Table 2: Fuel Quality Specs and Field Symptoms

Diesel cetane number45 â 55Hard cold start, white smoke, rough idleLost morning productivity

Water content< 200 mg/kgCorrosion, filter blockage, pump seizureRoadside breakdown
Particulate contaminationISO 4406 cleanScored injectors, bore wearShortened overhaul interval

Source: Compiled from EN 228 (petrol) and EN 590 (diesel) fuel specifications; Kenyan and Nigerian national fuel standards (KEBS EAS 158:2019; SON NIS 302:2018); Bosch Automotive Handbook (2018).

â  SAFETY WARNING â HIGH-PRESSURE FUEL & HOT EXHAUST

Never crack open a high-pressure diesel injection line while the engine is cranking or running. Common-rail and unit-injector systems on 6â12 litre engines can reach 1,800â2,500 bar â a jet of diesel can penetrate skin and cause diesel injection injury, which requires immediate hospital treatment. Equally, exhaust manifold surface temperatures on a loaded turbo-diesel reach 500â700 Â°C: keep dry grass, spilled diesel, and oily rags away from the manifold and turbo. In dusty African operating conditions, always depressurise the fuel system and allow the engine to cool for at least 30 minutes before opening any high-pressure component. Wear eye protection and gloves. Do not use bare hands to check for leaks â use a piece of cardboard.

Field Diagnostics: Turning Principles into Uptime

1. Thermodynamics of combustion. Heat released by burning fuel is converted to work only during the expansion stroke. The rest leaves as exhaust gas and coolant heat. Practically: monitor EGT and coolant temperature. A rising EGT on a constant load signals late injection, over-fuelling, or a restricted intake â all of which cut fuel economy and shorten turbo life. On a 12-litre haul truck in the DRC, a 40 Â°C EGT rise at the same gradient typically means a 5â8% fuel penalty.

2. Air-fuel mixtures and stoichiometry. Petrol engines must run close to stoichiometric (14.7:1) for the catalytic converter and oxygen sensor to work; diesel engines always run lean (18:1 to 70:1) because load is controlled by fuel quantity, not throttle. In dusty conditions â common across the Sahel, East African highlands, and Southern African dry season â a clogged air filter richens the mixture, raises EGT, and increases fuel consumption. Change intervals should be halved in high-dust operations. A cheap restriction indicator on the intake saves injector pumps.

3. Compression ratio. Higher compression raises thermal efficiency but also raises peak cylinder pressure and NOx. A worn engine with low compression shows hard cold starting, excessive blow-by, and blue/white smoke. Compression testing is a 20-minute job that prevents a full rebuild being scheduled too late. For agribusiness, a compression test on a standby generator before harvest season is cheap insurance.

4. Ignition timing and combustion phasing. In petrol engines, spark advance is calibrated for a specific octane. If you fill a 1990s Toyota 5L or a modern 1.5 L turbo with low-octane fuel, the knock sensor retards timing and you lose power and economy. In diesel engines, injection timing is set by the pump or ECU; a pump retarded by 2Â° costs cold-start performance and raises fuel consumption. Timing checks belong on every 500-hour service.

5. Knock and pre-ignition. Knock is the uncontrolled auto-ignition of end-gas in a petrol engine; pre-ignition is ignition before the spark. Both cause piston and valve damage. Symptoms: metallic rattle under load, power loss, rising coolant temperature. Causes: low octane, over-advanced timing, hot spots, lean mixture. In African fuel markets where octane can vary, retarding base timing 2â3Â° on older engines is a pragmatic mitigation.

6. Diesel combustion and ignition delay. Diesel ignites after a delay of roughly 0.5â2 milliseconds between injection and combustion. Long delay causes diesel knock, rough running, and higher NOx. Short delay is quieter and cleaner. Cetane number, injection pressure, and intake temperature all influence delay. Cold mornings in the Ethiopian highlands or South African winter make glow plugs and battery health business-critical.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Check air filter restriction weekly in dusty conditions; halve service intervals during harvest and dry season.
  2. Log EGT and coolant temperature daily on any engine above 3 litres â trends predict failures before they happen.
  3. Test fuel quality for water, particulate, and cetane/octane when changing suppliers or after long storage.
  4. Verify ignition/injection timing at every 500-hour service or after any pump/injector work.
  5. Run a compression test on any engine showing hard starting, blow-by, or excess oil consumption.
  6. Use the correct fuel grade â never assume "diesel is diesel" or "petrol is petrol" across borders.
  7. Train drivers on knock symptoms â a driver who reports pinging early saves an overhaul.
  8. Keep a fuel log per asset â litres per hour or per tonne-km is the single best health indicator.

Further Reading

  • U.S. Department of Energy â Internal Combustion Engine Basics (free, official).
  • NREL â Combustion and Engines Research (free, official).
  • U.S. EPA â Vehicle and Fuel Emissions Testing (free, official).
  • Bosch Mobility â Powertrain Solutions (free technical overviews).
  • Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) â Fuel Standards (free, official East African reference).

Rise AFRICA Skills â Engine Operating Principles module. Practical Reference lesson. Aligned to African agribusiness, transport, and off-grid power operations.

quiz.q: What is the stoichiometric air-fuel ratio for petrol by weight?
quiz.explanation: Petrol burns completely at 14.7 parts air to 1 part fuel by weight.

quiz.q: Which engine type uses a spark plug to ignite the air-fuel mixture?
quiz.explanation: Petrol engines use a spark plug; diesel engines rely on compression heat.

quiz.q: What is the typical compression ratio range for a diesel engine?
quiz.explanation: Diesel engines need high compression to ignite the fuel, typically 14:1 to 23:1.

quiz.q: What tool is used to measure compression in a cylinder?
quiz.explanation: A compression gauge screws into the spark plug or injector hole to measure pressure.

quiz.q: What does black smoke from a diesel exhaust usually indicate?
options: B) Too much fuel or not enough air
quiz.explanation: Black smoke is unburnt carbon from a rich mixture or restricted air intake.

quiz.q: What is ignition delay in a diesel engine?
options: A) Time between spark and combustion
B) Time between fuel injection and combustion
C) Time between intake and exhaust
D) Time between compression and injection
quiz.explanation: Ignition delay is the period from when fuel is injected to when it starts to burn.

quiz.q: Which of these can cause knock in a petrol engine?
quiz.explanation: Too much ignition advance causes the mixture to ignite too early, leading to knock.

quiz.q: What is pre-ignition?
quiz.explanation: Pre-ignition is when the mixture ignites before the spark plug fires, often due to a hot spot.

quiz.q: What is the typical base ignition timing for a petrol engine at idle?
quiz.explanation: Idle timing is usually 8-12 degrees before top dead centre.

quiz.q: What does a timing light measure?
quiz.explanation: A timing light flashes when the spark fires, showing the timing mark on the pulley.

quiz.q: What is the ideal peak pressure timing in a petrol engine?
quiz.explanation: Peak pressure should occur slightly after TDC to push the piston down efficiently.

quiz.q: Which fuel has a higher energy density by volume?
quiz.explanation: Diesel has about 10-15% more energy per litre than petrol.

quiz.q: What is the stoichiometric ratio for diesel by weight?
quiz.explanation: Diesel stoichiometric ratio is about 14.5 parts air to 1 part fuel.

quiz.q: Why do diesel engines not need a throttle plate?
options: A) They run at constant speed
B) They control power by fuel amount, not air
D) They have a spark plug
quiz.explanation: Diesel engines are unthrottled; power is controlled by how much fuel is injected.

quiz.q: What is the effect of running a petrol engine too rich?
options: A) Higher power and better economy
B) Fouled spark plugs and wasted fuel
quiz.explanation: Rich mixture leaves unburnt fuel that fouls plugs and wastes money.

quiz.q: What is the typical compression pressure for a healthy petrol engine?
quiz.explanation: Petrol engines usually read 10-14 bar (150-200 psi) on a compression gauge.

quiz.q: What does a wet compression test indicate if pressure rises?
quiz.explanation: If pressure rises after adding oil, the oil seals worn rings temporarily.

quiz.q: What is cetane number a measure of?
quiz.explanation: Cetane number indicates how easily diesel ignites; higher cetane means shorter delay.

quiz.q: What causes diesel knock?
quiz.explanation: Long ignition delay allows too much fuel to mix, causing a violent pressure rise.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a glow plug in a diesel engine?
options: B) To warm the combustion chamber for cold starts
quiz.explanation: Glow plugs heat the chamber to reduce ignition delay when the engine is cold.

quiz.q: Which exhaust smoke colour indicates burning oil?
quiz.explanation: Blue smoke is a sign of oil entering the combustion chamber.

quiz.q: What is the typical ignition delay in a diesel engine?
quiz.explanation: Ignition delay is usually 1-2 milliseconds in a warm diesel engine.

quiz.q: What happens if petrol engine ignition timing is too retarded?
quiz.explanation: Retarded timing causes the burn to finish late, losing power and raising exhaust temperature.

quiz.q: Which tool can help diagnose a misfiring cylinder in a diesel engine?
quiz.explanation: Cracking each injector line while running shows which cylinder is not contributing.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of high compression ratio in a diesel engine?
quiz.explanation: Higher compression extracts more work from the fuel, improving efficiency.

quiz.q: What is the risk of using low-octane petrol in a high-compression engine?
quiz.explanation: Low octane fuel ignites too easily under pressure, causing knock.

quiz.q: How can you reduce knock if only low-octane fuel is available?
quiz.explanation: Retarding timing delays the spark, reducing peak pressures that cause knock.

quiz.q: What does a vacuum gauge measure on a petrol engine?
quiz.explanation: Vacuum gauge reads manifold vacuum, which indicates engine health and mixture setting.

quiz.q: Which of these is a symptom of a blown head gasket?
options: A) High compression on all cylinders
B) Low compression on two adjacent cylinders
quiz.explanation: A blown head gasket often causes low compression between two neighbouring cylinders.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a knock sensor?
options: B) To detect knock and retard timing
quiz.explanation: The knock sensor listens for pinging and signals the ECU to retard timing.
